implementation_notes: In coroutine code the bulkhead is a suspending permit counter: Semaphore(n) per dependency, withPermit { } acquiring and releasing around the call (release is cancellation-safe because it runs in a finally), and tryAcquire() for the non-suspending fail-fast path. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by suspension: the bulkhead owns no threads, saturation parks coroutines in the semaphore's FIFO queue, so bound the number of waiters or use tryAcquire when rejection is required. Prefer the sibling dispatcher view when the dependency blocks a thread.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Semaphore with withPermit
variants.implementation_notes: In coroutine code the bulkhead is a suspending permit counter: Semaphore(n) per dependency, withPermit { } acquiring and releasing around the call (release is cancellation-safe because it runs in a finally), and tryAcquire() for the non-suspending fail-fast path. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by suspension: the bulkhead owns no threads, saturation parks coroutines in the semaphore's FIFO queue, so bound the number of waiters or use tryAcquire when rejection is required. Prefer the sibling dispatcher view when the dependency blocks a thread.
pitfalls: Semaphore waiters are unbounded; under sustained overload coroutines accumulate instead of failing, so cap waiting with tryAcquire or a timeout.
Do not run blocking JDBC or HTTP calls inside a semaphore-guarded suspend function on Dispatchers.Default - the permit bounds count, but blocked threads still starve the shared pool.
Releases belong inside withPermit or use; a manual acquire with an early return before release leaks a permit.
Creating a Semaphore per request or per call site defeats the bound; it must be shared per dependency.

variants.name: dedicated dispatcher view (limitedParallelism)
variants.implementation_notes: Thread-level isolation in coroutines: CoroutineDispatcher.limitedParallelism(n) returns a view of a dispatcher that runs at most n coroutines at a time, so wrapping a blocking dependency in withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8)) confines it to at most 8 of the IO threads and keeps the rest available for other work, without creating a private executor; keep the view as a per-dependency object. Use it instead of a semaphore when the dependency blocks threads (JDBC, file I/O): a semaphore counts tasks but does not reserve threads, whereas the view caps thread occupancy.
pitfalls: Cache the view instead of creating it per call: a fresh view each time multiplies effective thread usage.
Dispatchers.IO views are elastic, so many different views can still exhaust the shared IO pool; the cap protects the view, not the whole process.
Wrapping a suspending call in a limited view wastes concurrency because it holds a thread while suspended - use it only for genuine blocking work.
limitedParallelism needs kotlinx.coroutines 1.6+; older versions must use newFixedThreadPoolContext (deprecated) or a semaphore.
